title: Formed vs unformed: charity is external improper form making faith meritorious
source_text: IV. Eodem redit distinctio in Scholis Romanis plurimum usitata, per quam fidem distinguunt in formatam atque informem. Nam fidem informem vocant illam quae sola est & sine charitate, fidem vero formatam illam quae est cum charitate & dilectione conjuncta. Docent enim charitatem esse fidei formam, non quidem internam & proprie dictam, quae fidei absolute & in se consideratae essentiam constituat; sed formam quandam externam & improprie dictam, quae esse quoddam externum & respectivum fidei tribuit; nempe quod prosit ad vitam aeternam, & sit, ut loquuntur, salutis meritoria.
pass_a_gloss: To the same thing comes back the distinction most used in the Roman Schools, by which they distinguish faith into formed and unformed. For they call unformed that faith which is alone and without charity, but formed that which is joined with charity and love. For they teach that charity is the form of faith, not indeed an internal and properly so-called form which would constitute the essence of faith absolutely and considered in itself; but a certain external and improperly so-called form which confers on faith a certain external and relative being; namely that it profits unto eternal life and is, as they speak, meritorious of salvation.
pass_b_english: The usual Roman School distinction is formed versus unformed faith: unformed is faith alone without charity; formed is faith joined to charity and love.

Charity is called faith's form — not an internal essence-constituting form, but an external, improper form that gives faith a relative standing: it profits to eternal life and is, they say, meritorious of salvation.

lemmas.gloss: a certain external and improperly so-called form

choices.why: Blocks reading charity as faith's essence.
rejected: charity as substantial form of faith
